r1-p01-003: In April 2023, the walkway of the roughly 30-year-old Jeongja Bridge in Bundang suddenly collapsed while citizens were walking across it, killing one person and injuring another. The collapse of a bridge that looked intact from the outside was linked to corrosion and damage that had accumulated over a long period in its cantilever members. Warning signs such as cracking and sagging had been observed in inspections before the accident but did not lead to sufficient repair or reinforcement. This case shows that the mere existence of periodic inspection makes it difficult to track changes in structural condition continuously. Sudden collapses of aging bridges in service are not unique to Jeongja Bridge. The collapse of the Fern Hollow Bridge in Pittsburgh, USA, in January 2022 is a case in which progressive corrosion had already been flagged in periodic inspections, but repairs were delayed and the bridge finally fell while in use during the morning commute, revealing that having passed periodic inspections alone does not prevent accidents.
r1-p01-006: The two cases show that internal damage such as corrosion, cracking and fatigue can progress over long periods in aging bridges in service. Because such damage can lead to changes in dynamic properties such as stiffness, damping and natural frequency, it may be observable as an anomaly through vibration-based monitoring. However, a structure's vibration characteristics change not only with actual damage but also with environmental variables such as temperature and humidity, so even when a change in vibration is observed it is hard to tell whether it comes from damage or from environmental change. The problem therefore remains that periodic inspection alone can hardly capture, continuously between inspections, dynamic changes that do not show on the surface, and that separating environmental effects from observed vibration changes to pick out anomalies is also not easy.
r1-p01-007: According to the Korea Authority of Land & Infrastructure Safety's 2025 statistics by facility class, Korea has 37,543 bridges — 5,392 Class 1, 7,925 Class 2 and 24,226 Class 3 — of which Class 3 bridges account for about 64.5%. This shows that the scope of safety management extends not only to large bridges but also to relatively small ones. The need for low-cost continuous screening technology applicable to small and medium bridges is therefore growing.
r1-p02-002: As the need for safety management of aging and vulnerable facilities grew, the scope of precision safety diagnosis was also expanded from December 4, 2025. Class 2 facilities rated D or E in a precision safety inspection, and Class 2 and 3 facilities rated C, D or E in a safety inspection that had not received a precision safety diagnosis since 30 years after completion, were added to its scope. Precision safety diagnosis, however, remains a costly and labor-intensive procedure performed only on a fixed cycle — every 4 to 6 years depending on the safety grade — so a time gap opens between inspections during which the condition is not checked. If dynamic changes in a structure accumulate slowly during this gap while it passes visual inspection, they are hard to detect before the next inspection. As a result, pedestrian overpasses, small footbridges and aging small and medium bridges lack a low-cost supplementary means of continuously detecting changes in condition between inspections.
r1-p02-005: Existing SHM (Structural Health Monitoring) systems often rely on precision measurement equipment such as ultra-precise piezoelectric accelerometers, high-performance data-acquisition hardware, cloud-based analysis infrastructure or distributed fiber-optic sensors. For example, the smart fiber-optic BOCDA sensor of the Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS) has the advantage of precisely measuring strain and load position in a structure. Because such precision sensor systems require fiber-optic measurement infrastructure and dedicated equipment, however, their cost and installation constraints make them hard to apply widely and cheaply to small and medium aging bridges already in service. As a result, low-cost screening technology that can continuously monitor changes in the condition of small and medium bridges before the precision-diagnosis stage is effectively missing. Bridge safety management therefore needs a multi-stage concept in which continuous screening (first stage) filters out anomaly candidates before precision safety inspection and diagnosis. If low-cost screening fills this first stage, limited inspection staff and budgets can be concentrated on suspect bridges where anomaly candidates have been observed.
r1-p03-001: This work aims to address the three problems summarized above: that periodic inspection alone can hardly capture, continuously, dynamic changes that do not show on the surface; that there is no means of continuously detecting changes in condition that accumulate between inspection cycles; and that existing precision measurement systems are hard to apply widely and cheaply to small and medium aging bridges. This work, however, is not a system that predicts collapse directly or replaces precision safety diagnosis. It is a low-cost first-stage (supplementary) screening system that observes vibration characteristics together with environmental variables using a low-cost MEMS accelerometer and a temperature/humidity sensor, compensates for normal variation explainable by temperature and humidity, detects the remaining anomaly candidates early, and indicates which structures should be prioritized for precision inspection. In other words, it does not replace precision diagnosis but is positioned as a supplementary means of filling the time gap between periodic inspection and precision diagnosis. The purpose of this work is to develop a low-cost, machine-learning-based bridge vibration screening system that addresses both the continuous-monitoring blind spot of small and medium bridges and the absence of low-cost screening technology. The specific goals are three. First, collect vibration data using an ADXL355Z-based MEMS accelerometer and a Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+. Second, record temperature and relative humidity with a DHT22 sensor and learn the relationship between temperature/humidity and natural frequency from normal-state data to reduce false alarms caused by environmental change. Third, implement an explainable alarm system that, rather than simply outputting whether there is an anomaly, also shows in which frequency band (or band around a mode) the normal baseline was departed from.
r1-p03-002: The reasons for the three goals are as follows. First, it is practically difficult to obtain training data containing both normal and anomalous states, because damaged-state data cannot be created deliberately on a bridge in service; this work therefore adopts unsupervised learning trained only on normal data. Next, temperature/humidity compensation is needed because a bridge's natural frequency rises and falls naturally with air temperature and humidity even without damage [2]. Mistaking this natural variation for damage increases false alarms, so the part explained by temperature and humidity must be removed first and only the remaining change examined. Finally, the alarm must be explainable because a single “anomaly” signal makes it hard for field inspectors to judge where to look more closely. The system therefore also shows in which band the normal baseline was departed from, helping to set the direction of the follow-up precision inspection.
r1-p03-004: The core technology of this work is unsupervised anomaly detection on vibration data. When the acceleration sensor measures vibration, a machine-learning model first learns the vibration patterns of the normal state and then judges vibration that departs strongly from those patterns to be an anomaly candidate. Because simple anomaly detection alone leaves the problem of false alarms caused by environmental change, the following three functions are combined.
r1-p03-005: 1. Low-cost vibration measurement: the x-, y- and z-axis acceleration of the model bridge is recorded with an ADXL355Z-based 3-axis MEMS accelerometer module and a Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+. Because this work uses a foam-board model, the emphasis is on fixing the sensor firmly against the structure; for application to a real steel bridge, a magnetic bracket can also be used.
r1-p03-006: 2. Environmental compensation: normal variation due to the environment is first compensated using the relationship between temperature/humidity and vibration characteristics learned from normal data, and only the residuals not explained by temperature and humidity are used for anomaly detection. This reduces false alarms caused by environmental change.
r1-p03-007: 3. Explainable alarms: when an anomaly is detected, the system does not output only an overall anomaly score but visualizes in which frequency band (or band around a mode) a large reconstruction error occurred. The system does not definitively diagnose the cause of damage; it provides interpretive information so that field inspectors can judge the direction of the follow-up precision inspection. The concrete signal-processing, regression-compensation and anomaly-detection procedure that links these three functions from data collection to output is covered step by step in 2.3 Operating Principle.
r1-p03-010: An SHM study combined a Raspberry Pi with a low-cost MEMS accelerometer (ADXL355) and showed that a structure's natural frequencies, mode shapes and damping can be identified without ultra-precise piezoelectric sensors costing tens of millions of won [1]. That study, however, focuses on identifying dynamic
r1-p04-000: characteristics and does not separately address how environmental variables such as temperature and humidity, or changes in operational loading such as vehicle traffic, affect anomaly detection. This work introduces an environment-adaptive pipeline that learns the relationship between temperature/relative humidity and natural frequency by multivariate regression and then performs residual-based anomaly detection, reducing false alarms caused by temperature/humidity change.
r1-p04-002: The BOCDA (Brillouin Optical Correlation Domain Analysis) fiber-optic sensor system developed by the Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS) uses optical fiber to precisely measure strain and load position in a structure [4]. It has the advantage of identifying deformation or load concentration at specific points with high spatial resolution. This work, by contrast, aims not at fiber-based precision strain measurement but at continuously observing changes in a structure's dynamic vibration characteristics with a low-cost MEMS accelerometer. The two technologies therefore differ in the physical quantity measured and their purpose, and this work focuses on low-cost first-stage alerts and on indicating precision-inspection priorities for small and medium bridges.
r1-p04-004: The Swiss Z24 Bridge Benchmark provided by KU Leuven is one of the most widely used public datasets in vibration-based SHM and includes long-term monitoring data and progressive damage-test data [3]. Recently, many unsupervised models — Autoencoder, One-Class SVM, Isolation Forest, VAE and others — have been compared on the Z24 dataset [5][6]. Most of these studies, however, stop at outputting an anomaly score or whether a threshold is exceeded. This work decomposes the Autoencoder's reconstruction error by input feature or frequency band to visualize in which band the normal baseline was strongly departed from, and compares anomaly scores before and after temperature/humidity compensation to distinguish normal variation explainable by environmental variables from unexplained structural anomaly candidates.
r1-p04-006: The openLAB Research Bridge public dataset, from the long-term monitoring of a full-scale research bridge in Bautzen, Germany, includes environmental measurements such as air temperature and humidity along with acceleration responses, making it well suited to analyzing how seasonal change and daily temperature ranges affect a structure's vibration characteristics (dataset details in 2.7) [8]. The contribution of this work, however, is not the result of analyzing public data but the linking of low-cost sensor-based data collection, temperature/humidity compensation, anomaly judgment and band-wise explanation into one pipeline. The experiment on our own model bridge collects real data with an ADXL355Z, a DHT22 and a Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+ and confirms changes in vibration characteristics with changes in mass distribution. openLAB is used as supplementary validation data to check whether this environmental-compensation principle also holds on long-term monitoring data from a full-scale bridge. This study is therefore distinctive in that it is not a reanalysis of public data alone but a screening system that combines a low-cost hardware implementation with validation on public data from a full-scale bridge.
r1-p04-007: These distinctions can be summarized along three axes: direct low-cost hardware implementation, temperature/humidity compensation, and band-wise explainability. Unlike low-cost MEMS studies, this work reduces false alarms through temperature/humidity compensation; unlike fiber-optic measurement, it performs continuous screening with inexpensive general-purpose parts; and unlike unsupervised studies that output only an anomaly score, it also reports the contribution of each band to the reconstruction error.
r1-p04-009: This system is a supplementary vibration-screening system for early detection of vibration-anomaly candidates in aging small and medium bridges, based on low-cost, low-power hardware and unsupervised learning. It aims to collect vibration, temperature and relative humidity
r1-p05-000: with an ADXL355Z-based MEMS accelerometer and a DHT22 temperature/humidity sensor, and to reduce environment-driven false alarms using the temperature/humidity–frequency relationship learned in the normal state. It then detects anomaly candidates that depart from the normal vibration pattern with Autoencoder-based unsupervised learning and, when an anomaly occurs, shows which frequency bands (or bands around modes) have large reconstruction errors, helping to prioritize precision inspection.
r1-p05-003: The system is built as a hardware acquisition unit and a software analysis unit. The hardware acquisition unit consists of an ADXL355Z-based 3-axis MEMS accelerometer module, a DHT22 temperature/humidity sensor [7], a Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+, a power supply and a foam-board bridge model. Because the Raspberry Pi can store data on its own microSD card, a separate microSD storage module is optional rather than required.

r1-p05-027: The software analysis unit consists of an acquisition program and an analysis program. The acquisition program runs in Python on the Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+, receiving 3-axis acceleration from the ADXL355Z-based MEMS accelerometer at 200 Hz and temperature and relative humidity from the DHT22 at about 2-second intervals, and writes them to a single CSV file. The analysis program takes this file, splits the signal into fixed time windows, performs FFT and feature extraction, and then proceeds through residual calculation by multivariate regression on temperature T and relative humidity RH, standardization, reconstruction-error-based anomaly scoring, a 99th-percentile threshold decision, and a band-contribution plot. Because the two programs are linked by the same CSV format, the flow runs from collection to decision and explanation without any separate conversion step.
r1-p05-029: The ADXL355Z accelerometer is attached at the lengthwise center of the model bridge. With the full span of the model L and its width B, the default sensor position is x = L/2, y = B/2. In a simply supported model bridge the first bending response is largest at mid-span, so when only a single accelerometer is used, mid-span is the best place to observe changes in the dynamic properties of the whole structure. The sensor is fixed with its x axis along the bridge, its y axis across it and its z axis vertical; vibration features are computed for all three axes, but the z axis, which best reflects vertical bending, is the main axis of analysis.
r1-p05-030: Because the DHT22 is not a vibration sensor, it is not placed on the model bridge itself but in the same test environment within 3–10 cm of the ADXL355Z. It is mounted on a small fixed stand beside the bridge to record temperature and relative humidity without affecting the model's mass or stiffness. The Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+ is likewise not placed on the bridge but on a table or fixed stand beside it. Sensor cables are fixed near the supports with a little slack around the sensor so that cable tension does not affect the vibration response.

r1-p06-002: 1. Vibration and temperature/humidity acquisition: acceleration data are collected from the ADXL355Z-based 3-axis MEMS accelerometer, and temperature T and relative humidity RH are recorded from the DHT22. In the model-bridge experiment, the actual natural-frequency range is first checked in a preliminary test by tapping the model, and if necessary the analysis band is extended up to 100 Hz, the Nyquist limit of the 200 Hz sampling rate.
r1-p06-003: 2. Signal preprocessing and frequency-band feature extraction: the DC offset is removed from the time-domain acceleration signal, band-pass filtering is applied where necessary, and the frequency spectrum is computed with FFT or STFT. For each analysis segment and axis, RMS, standard deviation, peak-to-peak, spectral entropy, peak frequency and peak power, and band energies (default 0–3, 3–10, 10–20 Hz) are computed, and temperature T and relative humidity RH are used as model inputs or for environmental compensation. In a simply supported model bridge the z-axis peak frequency indicates the first natural frequency, so the first natural frequency is estimated from this peak. On the model bridge, the band boundaries can be adjusted to the peak frequency observed in the normal-state preliminary test. The band-wise analysis is used not to locate damage directly but as an auxiliary indicator explaining which vibration characteristic departed from the normal baseline.
r1-p06-004: 3. Multivariate regression compensation of the normal natural frequency by temperature and humidity: on normal-state data, a multivariate regression model is trained with temperature T and relative humidity RH as explanatory variables to predict the first natural frequency of the healthy structure. At inference, the current temperature and humidity are fed into the regression model to compute the normal-state prediction f̂ = g(T, RH), and the difference from the measurement, r = f − f̂, is defined as the residual corrected for the temperature/humidity effect. In this work, the same (T, RH) regression and residual calculation are applied not only to the first natural frequency but to each of the vibration features extracted above, and the resulting residual features together form the input to the anomaly-detection model. Because these residuals can include not only structural anomaly candidates but also sensor noise, changes in mounting and operational loading, they are used in this study as a criterion for detecting anomaly candidates rather than as a confirmation of damage.
r1-p06-005: 4. Unsupervised anomaly detection with an Autoencoder: the Autoencoder is trained only on residual features from the normal state. Normal data are reconstructed well, while data that depart from the normal pattern have a large reconstruction error. The anomaly threshold is set at an upper percentile (default 99th) of the reconstruction-error distribution of normal validation data. Each residual feature is standardized before training so that features with different units are reflected evenly. Because the model compresses the input into a low-dimensional latent representation and reconstructs it, it learns only the correlation structure of normal data. Since both training and thresholding use only normal data, continuous screening can begin without obtaining any damage data.
